ELI5: I'm assuming it's incredibly dark out where Pluto is. How do we get these pictures where the entire planet looks like it's lit up with a spotlight?

You can take photos of very dimly lit things by doing a long exposure or stacking lots of short exposure images (it helps to have a large aperture lens, but if you can run your exposure long enough even that doesn't matter too much). Doesn't work very well on moving objects, but if there are photons, a long enough exposure will capture enough to have a photo of any brightness you desire.
How can they take long exposure photos of the planet with the spacecraft traveling so fast? I mean, is it that far away from Pluto that its high speed is not that significant?

Because what matters is the change in the angle over the exposure. Even travelling at 30,000 miles an hour means that at it's closest approach (7,800 miles) a 1 second photo would mean a change in the angle of Pluto to the camera of about 0.06 degrees. The Rule of 600 in astrophotography uses 0.1 degrees as an acceptable level of blur in star photos, so it's in the same ball park.

From further away, the exposures could be longer because the angle is changing less because the distance is large relative to the speed of the probe.

You have to understand the light gradient of space. Given only visible light, the dark parts are REALLY DARK. This means that any light out there will shine like a beacon. Even the little light that reflects off of the sun will, in contrast, shine nice and "brightly."

That, plus extended exposure (a camera technique that leaves the "lens" open for longer to give it more time to absorb more light) images, you can get a pretty bright image of a planet that's 4.5 billion miles from the sun.
